lesson.title: Where Two Lines Meet: Solving Systems of Equations
lesson.summary: A system of equations is a set of equations considered together, and solving one means finding the point or points that satisfy every equation in the set at once.
lesson.body:
A single linear equation, like y equals 2x plus 1, has infinitely many solutions, since any ordered pair on that line satisfies it. A system of equations asks a stricter question: what ordered pair, or pairs, satisfies two or more equations at the exact same time. When each equation in the system is linear, its graph is a line, and the solution to the system is the point where those lines cross, since that intersection point is the only ordered pair lying on every line at once. If the lines never cross, because they are parallel, the system has no solution, and if the two equations describe the exact same line, every point on it is a solution.

One reliable method for solving a system is substitution, which works especially well when at least one equation is already solved for a variable. Consider this system: y equals 2x plus 1, and y equals negative x plus 7. Both equations already give y directly in terms of x, so set the two expressions equal to each other, since they both equal the same y at the solution point: 2x plus 1 equals negative x plus 7. Add x to both sides to gather the x-terms: 3x plus 1 equals 7. Subtract 1 from both sides: 3x equals 6. Divide both sides by 3: x equals 2. Substitute x = 2 back into either original equation to find y, using the first one: y equals 2 times 2 plus 1, which is 4 plus 1, equals 5. The solution is the point (2, 5). Check it in the second equation too: y equals negative 2 plus 7, which is 5, confirming the same y-value, so (2, 5) truly satisfies both equations at once.

A second method, elimination, works well when the equations are lined up in standard form and adding or subtracting them cancels a variable. Consider the system: 2x plus y equals 11, and x minus y equals 1. Notice the y-terms are positive y in one equation and negative y in the other, so adding the two equations straight down eliminates y entirely: (2x plus x) plus (y minus y) equals (11 plus 1), which simplifies to 3x equals 12, so x equals 4. Substitute x = 4 into the second equation: 4 minus y equals 1, so subtracting 4 from both sides gives negative y equals negative 3, and multiplying both sides by negative 1 gives y equals 3. The solution is (4, 3). Check both equations: 2 times 4 plus 3 is 8 plus 3, equals 11, correct, and 4 minus 3 equals 1, also correct.

Both methods always produce the same kind of answer, an ordered pair that makes every equation in the system true simultaneously, and both rely entirely on the equation-solving skills you already have. Choosing between substitution and elimination is mostly a matter of convenience: substitution is natural when a variable is already isolated, while elimination is natural when the equations are already aligned in standard form with matching or opposite coefficients ready to cancel.

Geometrically, the solution point (2, 5) from the first example is exactly where the two lines y equals 2x plus 1 and y equals negative x plus 7 cross when graphed, since that is the only ordered pair lying on both lines simultaneously. A system with two truly different slopes, as in that example, always has exactly one such intersection, and therefore exactly one solution.
